queue.title: Managing Large Projects: One Version of the Truth
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses large project governance, key data-consistency practices, and consequences for delivery.

Project decisions break down when finance, legal, technology, and operations work from different data.

A major project doesn't fail only from poor execution. It fails when teams understand the deadline, budget, scope, or acceptance criteria differently.

One version of the truth means every key data point has a source, an owner, a date, a status, and a change history. A meeting then serves decision-making, not arguing over which number is correct.

Every project must have an accountable person, an operational coordinator, legal and financial oversight, and a clear escalation procedure.

Worker output should be organised around deliverables and evidence, not the volume of activity.

queue.title: Currency Risk in International Business
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses currency risk, key hedging practices, and consequences for international business economics.

Revenue, costs, and financing in different currencies can change a project's economics even without any change in operating performance.

A company can meet its operating plan and still lose margin due to an exchange-rate change. Currency exposure arises at the moment of contracting, not only when an invoice is paid.

Risk management begins with mapping revenue, costs, debt, and capital investment by currency and by deadline.

Protection doesn't mean eliminating every change, but limiting the consequences to a level the project and the group can bear.

Contract clauses, natural flow matching, and financial instruments must all be part of a single plan.

queue.title: Speed Without Control Is Not Innovation
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Technology speeding up a wrong decision does not create progress, it increases the cost of error. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Technology that speeds up a wrong decision doesn't create progress, it increases the cost of the error.

Speed is useful only when an organisation knows what it's speeding up. Automating an unclear process means producing more errors in less time.

Technology that accelerates a wrong decision does not create progress, it simply raises the cost of the mistake — a distinction organisations too often forget when judging a new tool's value purely by execution speed.

Leadership that measures automation's success only by the number of cases processed per minute, without an equally serious measure of how many of those cases were processed correctly, is measuring the wrong thing — and that mistake surfaces only after the damage is already done.

Real innovation must improve the outcome, demonstrability, and accountability. Everything else is technological decoration.

Management must not hand the final decision to a system that can't explain its data source and the limitations of its own result.

Management that measures the success of automation solely by the number of cases processed per minute, without an equally serious measure of how many were processed correctly, is measuring the wrong thing.

The correction is not to slow innovation down for its own sake, but to ensure that speed and accountability are evaluated together, so that an initiative is judged not only by how fast it moves but by whether anyone can explain and defend the results it produces.
